problems.one_liner: Each node holds a child map plus an end-of-word flag.
problems.core_objective: Implement a prefix tree supporting insert, search, and startsWith.
problems.bounds: lowercase English letters only, so at most 26 children per node. With 1e4 words of length 100 the node count can reach 1e6, which makes per-node memory the real constraint in Python.

approaches.name: 26-array trie (BEST for a fixed lowercase alphabet)
approaches.aha: Node = { children[26], isEnd }. children[i] is the child for letter 'a'+i; isEnd marks where an inserted word terminates. insert : walk letters, allocate missing children, set isEnd. search : walk letters; missing child ⇒ false; return isEnd. startsWith: walk letters; missing child ⇒ false; else true — NO isEnd check, any descendant counts.
approaches.py:
self.children: List[Optional["SolutionOne._Node"]] = [None] * 26
    self.isEnd: bool = False  # True = a word terminates here
self.root: SolutionOne._Node = SolutionOne._Node()
node = self.root
for ch in word:
    idx = ord(ch) - 97  # 'a'→0 … 'z'→25 — one multiply to find child
    if node.children[idx] is None:
        node.children[idx] = SolutionOne._Node()  # grow the path

approaches.why: Follows directly from the traversal count: O(L) per op — L = word length. time, O(26·n·L) worst case — n·L nodes, each holding space.

approaches.name: Hash set + linear prefix scan (contrast)
approaches.aha: Store every word verbatim in a Python set (open addressing with LINEAR PROBING: h(k, i) = (hash(k) + i) mod m, i = 0, 1, 2, …). search : O(1) average — one probe sequence. startsWith: scan ALL stored words and prefix-compare each — O(n·L), because a hash set cannot answer prefix queries.
approaches.py:

self.words.add(word)
return word in self.words
return any(w.startswith(prefix) for w in self.words)
approaches.why: one O(1) hash probe per element, no rescans; hence the stated bounds.

problems.cpp_vs_py:
The trie is a 26-way tree: every node has 26 child slots (one branch per letter position) + an isEnd flag. Words sharing a prefix share EVERY node of that prefix — "app" then "apple" costs only 2 extra nodes, not 5. Hash sets (dict/set probing h(k,i) = (hash(k)+i) mod m) give O(1) EXACT matches but cannot do prefix queries — a prefix is not a key. The trie converts them into a single O(L) walk at the price of memory: each node pre-allocates 26 slots (26×8 B ≈ 208 B) even when 1–2 children exist. Fixed small alphabet → list children (index = ord(c)-97); unbounded alphabets (Unicode) → dict children allocate only what is used. =====================================================================

cpp_alts: `vector<TrieNode>` with `children[26]` as a fixed array is cache-ideal but costs 104 bytes per node; a `map` or `vector<pair>` child list is denser for sparse nodes.
`gp_hash_table<char,int>` per node is a poor fit: one hash table per node is heavy, and 26 edges do not justify hashing.
py_alts: A plain `dict` per node is the standard; a `list` of 26 is faster for lookup but wastes memory on sparse tries.
`defaultdict(dict)` for children removes the membership test on insert.
A set of all words supports startsWith by scanning, but search becomes $O(\sum |w|)$ -- worse, though trivially correct.
problems.trap: Confusing search with startsWith: `search('app')` must require the end-of-word flag, `startsWith('app')` must not. Returning the node without checking the flag makes every prefix a word.
problems.invariant: Following the character sequence of a query reaches a node iff that sequence is a prefix of some inserted word. The flag at that node distinguishes "a word ends here" from "a path continues", which is the only difference between the two query methods.

questions.q: Why does a trie beat a set for startsWith?
questions.a: A set requires scanning all words or building a separate prefix structure, and a scan is $O(n)$ regardless of query length. A trie answers startsWith in $O(L)$ where L is the query length, independent of the number of words stored.

questions.q: What is the memory cost per node?
questions.a: A Python dict costs roughly 64 bytes empty and grows with entries, so a million-node trie can exceed 200 MB. C++ with `children[26]` costs 104 bytes plus the flag, but compresses into a flat array with child indices -- predictable and cache-friendly.

questions.q: How would you support arbitrary characters?
questions.a: Replace the fixed 26-array or lowercase assumption with a map, and index by code point rather than `ord(c) - ord('a')`. Unicode tries need care with surrogate pairs in narrow builds.

problems.one_liner: Treat '.' as a branch point during the descent.
problems.core_objective: Implement a trie supporting insert and a search that allows '.' to match any single character.
problems.bounds: 1 <= word.length <= 25 with lowercase letters and '.', at most 100 words stored. A query of all dots must not blow up -- without pruning it explores 26^d paths.

approaches.name: Trie + recursive DFS (best)
approaches.aha: Walk the trie with an index i into the pattern. pattern[i] == '.' → try EVERY child; true if any matches. pattern[i] == 'c' → follow only child 'c'; missing ⇒ false. i == len(pattern) → answer = isEnd of the current node. The '.' branch is O(26) per level worst case; letters stay O(1).
approaches.py:
self.root: _TrieNode = _TrieNode()
node = self.root
for ch in word:
    node = node.children.setdefault(ch, _TrieNode())  # grow path
node.isEnd = True  # mark word completion
    if i == len(word):
        return node.isEnd
    ch = word[i]
approaches.time: O(26^d) worst case, d = number of '.'; O(L)
approaches.space: O(26·n·L) trie nodes worst case + O(L) call stack.
approaches.why: every node is visited once and returns O(1) state; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: Trie + iterative BFS (level-by-level frontier)
approaches.aha: Keep a FRONTIER of candidate nodes. For each pattern char: '.' → frontier = ALL children of every candidate. 'c' → frontier = only the 'c'-children of candidates. Empty frontier ⇒ no match. Finally, true iff some surviving node has isEnd. Same complexity as DFS, no recursion stack, and every candidate advances in lockstep — the natural "wavefront" view.
approaches.py:
self.root: _TrieNode = _TrieNode()
node = self.root
for ch in word:
    node = node.children.setdefault(ch, _TrieNode())
node.isEnd = True
frontier: deque[_TrieNode] = deque([self.root])  # nodes alive so far
for ch in word:
    next_frontier: deque[_TrieNode] = deque()
approaches.time: O(26^d) worst case, O(L) without wildcards.
approaches.why: every node is enqueued and dequeued once; hence the stated bounds.

   root -> a exists; then '.' branches over b,d,m
     'a'+'d' exists ; third char 'd' exists -> flag? yes -> True
   -> 3 branches at ONE level only (the whole query has
      a single dot), so this is cheap

cpp_alts: Recursive DFS with `const vector<TrieNode*>& children` avoids copying the child vector per call.
Iterative DFS with an explicit stack bounds the stack at $O(L)$ regardless of the branching factor.
py_alts: `for c in children[node]:` iterates values directly, saving a dict lookup per child.
Recursion depth equals word length (25), so the default Python limit is never a concern here.
problems.trap: Not pruning when the '.' is the final character of the pattern. `26^L` is astronomically slow, and the fix is a one-line check that a node with any child satisfies a trailing wildcard.
problems.invariant: `search(node, i)` is true iff there is an inserted word matching `pattern[i:]` within node's subtree. The split into "pattern[i] == '.'" (try every child) and "concrete character" (take one child) covers exactly the wildcard semantics, so the recursion is exhaustive and sound.

questions.q: What is the worst-case time of the wildcard search?
questions.a: Exponential in the number of dots, up to $26^d$ for d dots. The trailing-dot optimisation caps it, and in practice LeetCode inputs keep dot counts low -- but stating the exponential bound and the pruning is the interview answer.

questions.q: Why does a trailing dot return immediately?
questions.a: Because any descendant of the current node completes the word. If the node has at least one child, some continuation exists and matches the single remaining dot. If it has no children, there is nothing to match. That test is exact, not a heuristic.

questions.q: How would you add prefix search with dots?
questions.a: Return true if the recursion reaches i == len(pattern) without failing -- whether or not a flag is set -- which is exactly `startsWith` generalised to wildcards.

problems.one_liner: Each trie node walks the grid instead of matching its word.
problems.core_objective: Find all words in a dictionary that exist in a grid using adjacent horizontal or vertical moves, each cell at most once per word.
problems.bounds: up to 3e4 cells, 1e5 words of length up to 10e3. Pruning is essential: without removing found words and without early termination the search is hopeless.

approaches.name: Trie + grid DFS backtracking (foundation)
approaches.aha: Build the trie (each terminal node stores its full word, which doubles as a "found" marker). For every cell, DFS: prune when the letter has no trie child; mark cells '#' while visiting to stop re-use, restore on backtrack. When a node's stored word is found, record it and CLEAR the stored word so it is never reported again.
approaches.cpp:
if (!child->word.empty()) {         // this path spells a full word
    found.push_back(child->word);   // report it…
    child->word.clear();            // …and never report it again
approaches.time: O(m·n·4^L) worst case — L = max word length,
approaches.why: every node is visited once and returns O(1) state; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: Trie + grid DFS with branch pruning (BEST)
approaches.aha: Same walk, plus a refs counter on every node = number of words still reachable through it. When a node's last remaining word is found, refs drops to 0 and the whole dead branch is DELETED from the trie — future DFS never re-explores it. This removes the classic "found word still costs DFS time on every later cell" waste.
approaches.time: O(m·n·4^L) worst case, faster in practice.
approaches.why: every node is visited once and returns O(1) state; hence the stated bounds.

problems.diagram:
grid:  oaan
        etaen
        iok
        le        words: [oath, pea, eat, rain]

  THE SHIFT: each trie node stores the LIST OF GRID CELLS
  where that prefix occurs. So one node does O(4) work per cell
  rather than rescanning its whole word.

   root: all (0,0) (0,1) (0,2) (0,3)
            (1,0)... (2,3)
   node 'o': (0,0) (1,0) (2,1)
   node 'oa': (0,0)
   node 'oat': (0,0) -> neighbour 'h' at (1,0)? no -> dead
   node 'e': (0,1) (1,1) (1,3) (2,2)
   node 'ea': (1,1)
   node 'eat': (1,1) -> 't' at (1,2)? yes -> flag -> 'eat' FOUND
              remove 'eat' from the trie (prune)

  per node work: 4 neighbours * (rows*cols) cells = O(4RC)
  marking is by mutating the CELL to '#' then restoring,
  so a cell is never reused within one path.
cpp_alts: Store `(row, col)` pairs per node in a `vector`; that is the algorithm's essential data, not an optimisation.
Deleting found words from the trie is the main pruning win -- without it every grid cell keeps searching for words already reported.
Encode positions as `int` instead of a pair to halve the node payload.
py_alts: A list of ints per node with `for p in node.positions:` avoids tuple unpacking.
Deleting from the trie: set the node's children to an empty list so the DFS stops descending there.
problems.trap: Forgetting to unmark the grid cell after the recursive call. The cell stays as '#' and every other word that needs it fails, so the answer is missing valid words.
problems.invariant: The list at trie node u holds exactly the grid cells where u's prefix ends, for the current search. DFS from u visits each such cell, marks it, and recurses into the child matching the next character. Marking makes the path self-avoiding; restoring after the loop restores the invariant for sibling branches.

questions.q: What does storing grid positions in the trie buy?
questions.a: It inverts the loops. Instead of every cell trying every dictionary word (O(RC * W)), each trie node does O(4) work per cell it occupies, so the total is proportional to the number of (prefix, cell) pairs that actually exist. Shared prefixes are explored once instead of once per word.

questions.q: Why is removing found words necessary?
questions.a: Without it, a cell visited late still descends the full remaining trie looking for words already reported, wasting the dominant share of the work. Removing a found word prunes that subtree for every later cell, and since the answer is a set, reporting twice is wrong anyway.

questions.q: How does marking prevent revisiting a cell?
questions.a: Temporarily writing '#' into the cell makes any check of its character fail for the remainder of that path. Because the recursion restores the original character on the way out, sibling branches still see the true letter -- so marking gives path-local, not global, exclusion.
